issues.explanation: 'Avoid Night' implies fear linked to darkness/outdoor danger, but there are no Threat items and no memory/trigger content tied to night-time, darkness, or outdoor contexts. For this relief-worker trauma, that strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the least coherent item because it addresses a threat context not otherwise represented across Triggers, Memory, or Negative Appraisals.

Yet the selected Threat items are central, high-intensity PTSD threat responses and are also mirrored elsewhere. This makes Threat functionally active in a way that contradicts the formulation structure.

issues.explanation: Threat: Flashbacks and Threat: Physical Reactivity are tightly linked to the Memory and Triggers nodes, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Threat. Including these as Threat items makes the profile inconsistent with the stated node architecture.

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Entrapment could occur, but here it lacks a clear connection to the rest of the selected content and weakens coherence.

This creates a contradiction with the formulation structure, especially given concurrent trigger and memory items that imply exactly the kind of reminder-linked threat activation the model marks as inactive. The other nodes are broadly coherent with each other and with the trauma type.

Threat has no active incoming or outgoing edges, so it should not appear as a tightly integrated maintaining component. Yet all three selected Threat items are non-specific PTSD symptom/severity indicators rather than a coherent sense of current threat, and they are not meaningfully linked to the active Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies pattern.

vignette: When 80-year-old Kumar Singh returned from the eastern front, the images of burnt villages and the cries of civilians still flickered behind his eyes. He had seen people acting with cruelty that violated every moral code he had known, and he felt trapped when, for days, his supplies ran out and the convoy could not move. Those moments of helplessness became the core of his nightmares, which roused him in the middle of the night with a sharp gasp. The very memory of those events - the smell of smoke, the sound of gunfire, the feeling that the world had become a hostile place - lodged itself as a living presence, replayed in a loop that made him feel as though he were back on the road, as though the past had seeped into the present. From the outset, these triggers drove him to avoid any news of current conflicts, rehearse every conversation he might have with family, and scan his surroundings for threats, as if a new bomb could drop at any moment. Because Kumar believed the world was dangerous, his appraisals turned increasingly dire. He worried that his reactions-his sudden anger when the office air conditioner blew off his screen, his irritability at his colleague's jokes-would prove he was going crazy. The thought that he might lose control and lash out in a fit of rage spurred him to rehearse each interaction, hoping that rehearsal would keep him calm. His fear that the world's violence was an omen of his own breakdown also heightened his vigilance; the knowledge that he might be losing his mind amplified his feeling of the memory as present. Thus, the same appraisals that kept him in a state of hyper-alertness also pushed him to avoid news, rehearse, and check his environment constantly, as a preemptive shield against an imagined loss of control. The relentless replay of that traumatic night continued to shape his strategies. Each time the film of the convoy's breakdown played, Kumar's mind flooded with images of people screaming, and he immediately began rehearsing his responses to any forthcoming conversation, fearing that a slip would trigger another outburst. His body, ever tense, tightened in anticipation of a danger that might not be real. The memory's vividness also re-ignited the sense of moral violation; each recollection of a child's terrified face became a new trigger for fear. As these memories resurfaced, they sent a signal back to his perception of threat, reinforcing his belief that the world was a battlefield and that every unfamiliar face might be a perpetrator. In turn, his maladaptive habits looped back onto his memories and his sense of danger. By deliberately avoiding news, he removed an opportunity for new information that might soothe or confirm his anxieties; instead, the absence heightened the gap, allowing the old memories to occupy the silence. Checking his surroundings became a ritual that, while meant to reassure him, actually sharpened his focus on every shadow, thereby making him more susceptible to interpreting benign events as moral violations or entrapments. The constant rehearsal of conversations, which he thought would keep him in control, ended up reinforcing the fear that if he spoke incorrectly he would provoke violence, thereby tightening the cycle of threat and memory. Kumar's day-to-day life as a data scientist had become a battlefield of its own. While he could still crunch numbers and debug code, the fear that his mind might falter, the anxiety that any small trigger could erupt into rage, and the bodily sense of constant alertness made even the quiet hum of a keyboard feel oppressive. When he finally sought help, it was because the irritability that erupted in meetings, the body-on-alert tension that left him physically exhausted, and the relentless replay of that war night that woke him in the middle of the night had become unbearable. He hopes to regain a sense of safety, to free himself from the endless rehearsals, and to believe, perhaps finally, that the world can be a place where he is not forever on guard.
